summary: SPHEREx SkyLens is a public web app that lets anyone watch the infrared sky change over time using real NASA SPHEREx data. You type a name ("Barnard's Star") or coordinates, or tap a place on the map, and SkyLens shows that patch of sky in any of SPHEREx's 102 infrared channels, or as a colour composite of a chosen wavelength range. A one-button timelapse plays the SPHEREx epochs as a short video, with blink and difference modes that make moving objects stand out, and overlays the expected track from Gaia proper motions. One tap builds a 0.75–5 µm spectrum of any point from the SPHEREx images themselves. Users can overlay AllWISE (2010) to see 15 years of motion, Gaia DR3 stars with motion arrows, and the asteroids and comets that crossed the field on each epoch date (JPL). Every view is a shareable URL, the app works in English and Spanish, installs as a PWA, and on phones can be pointed at the sky. It is built to ingest new SPHEREx releases automatically through IRSA, so it keeps working as data arrives.
details:
What it does. SkyLens turns SPHEREx's all-sky survey into something a non-specialist can explore in seconds. Enter coordinates or a name (or pick from well-known places such as the Andromeda Galaxy), choose a field of view from arcminutes to the whole sky, and browse the 102 infrared channels one at a time or as a colour composite of any wavelength range. The "timelapse" button fetches every SPHEREx image of that spot through IRSA, co-adds each six-month epoch, and plays them as a video; "blink" and "difference" modes make anything that moved or changed brightness jump out, and the expected path of known high-proper-motion objects is drawn on top. Tapping the sky identifies the nearest catalogued object (SIMBAD) in plain language, and one more tap builds its 0.75–5 µm spectrum directly from the SPHEREx images, with an explanation of what the dips mean. Overlays include AllWISE (to compare against 2010), Gaia DR3 with proper-motion arrows, a coordinate grid, and the asteroids and comets that crossed the field on each epoch date (JPL Small-Body Identification). Each image lists detector, wavelength range, date, data release and a link to the original FITS file. Every view, including channel range, mode and projection, lives in the URL, so results can be shared or embedded.

How it works. The front end is a React + TypeScript app (Vite) built on CDS Aladin Lite for sky rendering; images come from IRSA's SPHEREx HiPS cube and are served directly from IRSA for single channels, while a small FastAPI (Python, astropy, numpy) service composes multi-channel colour tiles, runs IRSA Simple Image Access searches, builds epoch co-adds and spectra from FITS cutouts, and caches results. The API queries IRSA live and groups observations into epochs automatically, so new SPHEREx releases (DR1, QR3 and the next ones) appear without code changes. The web app is a PWA (installable, offline shell) deployed on Azure Static Web Apps; the API runs on Azure Container Apps.

Who it is for and why it matters. The challenge is that SPHEREx produces more images than any person or pipeline can inspect; discoveries of comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and variable stars have historically come from volunteers comparing images by eye. SkyLens lowers the barrier to zero: no software to install, no catalogue names to know, two languages, keyboard and touch navigation, a phone mode that points at the real sky, and friendly explanations instead of jargon. It was tested on the five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis); for instance, Barnard's Star's 10″/yr motion is visible in the difference mode and as a 2.6′ offset against AllWISE, and WISE 0855's spectrum shows the water and methane absorption expected from the coldest known brown dwarf.

Design decisions. We kept the full 102-channel resolution available but default to single channels and sampled composites so the app stays fast on any connection; we use IRSA's own HiPS and SIA services rather than copying data, so the tool is cheap to run and always current; we show data provenance (detector, time, release, FITS link) and explain limitations honestly (e.g. R Draconis saturates the detector, so the app says so instead of showing an empty plot).
